Into The Gloom, developed by earrgames and published by Conglomerate 5, is an eerie and atmospheric first-person horror adventure that takes an unconventional approach to fear. Rather than relying on graphical realism or heavy narrative exposition, it builds unease through abstraction, mood, and a minimalist aesthetic that trades color for psychological weight. The entire experience unfolds in stark shades of black, white, and crimson, creating a sense of unreality that immediately disorients the player. You awaken in a strange, empty place, stripped of context and purpose, and are left to piece together the story through cryptic messages, environmental clues, and encounters with a menacing presence known only as The Shadow. The absence of explicit exposition enhances the tension, as each step forward feels like a descent deeper into something inexplicable and wrong.

The gameplay structure of Into The Gloom revolves around exploration, puzzles, and evasion. There is no combat, no weapon to rely on, and no safe refuge. The game’s design forces the player to embrace vulnerability, heightening the sense of fear and isolation. You traverse through a series of interconnected areas—hospitals, corridors, darkened rooms—solving environmental puzzles while avoiding The Shadow, whose sudden appearances keep you constantly on edge. These encounters rely more on sound design and anticipation than on jump scares. The audio cues are subtle but effective, with distant footsteps, doors creaking, and ambient distortions that make even empty spaces feel threatening. Each area you explore becomes a puzzle box of dread: claustrophobic, unpredictable, and always suggesting that something unseen is watching. The result is a rhythm of quiet exploration punctuated by moments of panic that keep you in a state of constant alertness.

What makes Into The Gloom distinctive is its aesthetic restraint. The monochromatic palette strips the world of warmth, making every red accent stand out with ominous significance. The visuals are deliberately lo-fi and pixelated, but this choice enhances the atmosphere rather than detracts from it. The blocky shapes and limited color depth evoke the feeling of being trapped in a nightmare—vague, distorted, and shifting between familiarity and abstraction. It recalls the era of early indie horror experiments, where imagination filled in the gaps left by minimal detail. The simplicity allows for creative tension; instead of showing horror directly, the game lets your mind conjure it. Coupled with haunting ambient music and muffled sound effects, the experience becomes immersive in a way that high-definition realism often fails to achieve. It’s a quiet, creeping dread rather than an explosive one, and it lingers long after you close the game.

The narrative unfolds slowly and obliquely. You are given fragments—notes, visions, symbolic imagery—but the story remains intentionally incomplete, leaving interpretation to the player. Themes of psychological torment, guilt, and fear of the unknown run through the experience. The multiple endings, five in total, suggest that choices and exploration can influence the outcome, though the differences between them are often subtle rather than drastic. This approach reinforces the sense of disorientation; the game isn’t about discovering a single truth but rather about feeling trapped in a looping nightmare where clarity is always out of reach. For those who enjoy ambiguity and environmental storytelling, this works beautifully, but players seeking a concrete plot may find the vagueness frustrating. The pacing can also test patience at times—some puzzles are trial-and-error, and the absence of clear direction means moments of aimless wandering are inevitable.

Despite its minimalism, Into The Gloom manages to achieve what many higher-budget horror titles do not: genuine tension born from atmosphere. The slow, deliberate pacing, the uncertainty of what’s around the corner, and the oppressive stillness all combine to create an unsettling psychological space. It’s the kind of horror that creeps under your skin, relying on suggestion rather than spectacle. However, this same restraint may limit its appeal. Some sections verge on repetition, and certain timed sequences or chase moments can feel frustrating due to their precision demands. The lack of polish in some puzzle logic and the occasional awkward pacing remind you of its indie origins. Yet these imperfections also lend it a certain authenticity—an unrefined but earnest creation that thrives on its rawness.

Into The Gloom stands as a small but memorable entry in the realm of indie horror. It’s a game that understands fear as something internal, a psychological weight rather than a loud shock. Its stylized visuals, minimalist storytelling, and haunting sound design combine to produce a uniquely oppressive atmosphere that lingers long after the credits roll. While not without flaws—its pacing, mechanical simplicity, and cryptic progression can alienate some players—it succeeds admirably within its scope. It’s a reminder that horror doesn’t need excess to be effective; sometimes all it takes is silence, darkness, and the feeling that you’ve wandered too far into a world you were never meant to see.

Into The Gloom is a fairly run of the mill "haunted hospital/house/apartment/asylumn" horror jumpscare first person adventure, with the specific differentiator here that the graphics are particularly terrible.  All you do is run around looking for objects and the odd page of text designed to make you feel uncomfortable, and comically run down hallways full of doors that are all locked/jammed/stuck etc etc... video games, a universe where 99% of doors just don't work. 

One important note is that even though this is an amateur project, it does seem to be sincerely and genuinely made.  I couldn't find any flipped assets, plagiarism or any other kind of insincere actions from the developer, but unfortunately genuine intentions alone are not enough to produce a brilliant PC gaming experience.  It's also worth noting that while some third party assets, mostly sound assets, were used in the game, the developer properly credited the creators of those assets.  See how easy it is to do the right thing and not be a plagiarist/asset flipper?  Kudos to the developer there.

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

The game features lazy low-polygon voxel "Minecraft"-like "art", making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the 1990s.  A lot of amateur developers see Minecraft's success and assume it's because it looks bad, not because it had unique and appealing game mechanics, and they try to emulate the success without understanding it.  It also happens to be easy, and doesn't need any proper talent in terms of game development/graphic artists etc.  That's why reviewers are faced with so many of these terrible games with confrontingly bad graphics.  Developers must learn that Minecraft succeeded despite the bad graphics, not because of them.

You don't have to take my word about how bad the game is, we can measure the interest in a game by how much people bothered to play it.  Into The Gloom has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game absolutely failed to capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for escaping the maze, trivial to achieve, but less than 7 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  That's a tiny, tiny proportion of gamers who even bothered with this.  Ouch.

Reviewing SteamDB to check how popular this game was with players reveals a surprise... there's a modest spike in player counts for the game.  But this only happened once, and isn't consistent with the achievement stats, that show less than 7 percent of players bothered playing the game for any reasonable amount of time.  How is it possible for this game to have so many concurrent players who didn't bother engaging with this game?  Trading cards.  People will use card idling software to collect the cards and sell them, but this won't trigger any achievements in-game.

That tells us people only really bought this game for trading cards, and that's a damning indictment of the woeful quality.  A closer look at the numbers shows the game just has a couple of players every week running up the game and idling it for cards, then deleting it.  We must ask how it benefits gamers for there to be so many games like this, with little merit as a serious game, that only generate sales from people idling and selling the trading cards.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Into The Gloom is relatively cheap at $3 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  This is also competing with over 11,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

While I'm giving this game a recommendation, my feelings on the overall experience are mixed. I'll start with the positives.

Aesthetically, the game pulls off the minimalist pixelated look using only shades of monochrome and a blood red color. This gives the areas an intensely ethereal appearance on par with old 32-bit horror games. It also has great sound design, knowing when to add more tension or relief into an area's atmosphere. Many of the puzzles are well thought out.

Now, the negatives. The pause feature doesn't really work, as monsters can still move and kill you while "paused." The level design of each area can be all over the place; often, there are many labyrinthine corridors with too many dead ends and locked doors. Notes and important items can sometimes blend in with the environment, making it difficult to backtrack and see what you're actually missing.

There are a total of 5 endings: [spoiler]two of which are death-related, two that rely on whether you complete a specific optional puzzle in the game or not, and one secret ending that you can only get a hint on how to achieve by finding a note in a Rebirth playthrough.[/spoiler] I'm cool with having multiple endings as they do give this game some replay value.

However, there's one major flaw. Even though the game does seem to be structured by chapters/areas, there is no actual chapter select. There's only one save file, so you can't go back to an earlier point in your playthrough. If you're a completionist and trying to get all achievements, you know where I'm going with this; if you miss ANYTHING and can't backtrack, you'd have to start a new playthrough to try again.

Ideally, you can complete everything the game offers you in just two full playthroughs. But to find out how to get the secret ending without looking up a guide, you need to do a Rebirth playthrough; if you do an Awakening playthrough first, you're probably going to end up with three separate playthroughs minimum just to get that last ending.

The final area [spoiler]in the Rebirth story path is also poorly designed and frustrating. To survive it, you'd pretty much have to speedrun it without knowing what you're supposed to do next. You get a short time limit to solve some puzzles, then explore a large area to find collectibles and wherever you're supposed to go and avoid the monsters. The ending also feels like a major slap in the face after going through more work, feeling like a hollow victory for the protagonist and places him into yet another less-than-ideal fate.[/spoiler]

Overall, a decent pixel horror title with some glaring flaws.

[h1]SUMMARY[/h1]
So originally when I played this game, I got about as far as the outside, near apartment buildings I think, and I got stuck. Years later, after being finished and removed from Early Access, I play it again and I find myself completely disinterested in it.

The tone of the game lives up to its namesake, the environment being filled with nothing but red, black, and white, giving the game a very morbid color palette. One of the first things it has you do is finding a keycode for a door. Mistake number 1 was making that keycode on a piece of paper you can easily look over in an area you would've never thought to look and would easily walk right by, as only its gray outline is visible to tell it apart from the table it's laying on. When you're designing puzzles, DO NOT make items blend in with the environment if they are vital to progression. That doesn't mean circle them with a huge neon color and have an arrow point to them, it means use some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ common sense and not make an item camouflaged with the environment. If you're using a restricted color palette, then think of a better place to put it where the player might think to actually look, not on any old table in the cafeteria.

Mistake number 2 was having a single random door that was previously locked, unlock, after you pick up a certain item. If you do this, you aren't just a ♥♥♥♥ game designer, you're an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Forcing the player to search for doors that unlocked after picking up an item, 5 minutes in, is a sure-fire method to being well on your way towards earning the hatred of the player. If I wanted to go Easter egg hunting, I'd wait till Easter and get in my kiddie outfit with my plastic basket and go easter egg hunting with all the other 10 year olds. DON'T DO THIS.

Mistake number 3 was including a tile puzzle as a part of your required progression. You remember playing Resident Evil 4? That game was great, wasn't it? How it was filled with a tense atmosphere, creepy enemies, and innovative gameplay? Yea, you remember that part of the game literally every single person doesn't remember because they block it out because of how much it slowed the game down and was utterly a crock of ♥♥♥♥? Yea, it was the tile puzzle you were forced to solve with Ashley. NOBODY LIKES THESE. They are time wasting filler used to slow progression to a halt, and god forbid the tile puzzle doesn't reset, other-wise you're completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥. On top of it being a tile puzzle, you're not even given the order in which to set the tiles in the first place.

Mistake 4 was having a level layout that is purposely confusing. You have 45 degree angle hallway intersections, Y shaped intersecting corridors that lead around in a circle, with lots of small branching hallways. Compounded onto this is the fact that every looks the same and you're left going in circles for a minute or two or, god help you if you come back to this game after a week or so and don't recall exactly what you were doing and exactly where you were.

This game screams "amateur hour" and then tries to rub your nose in it, and I refuse.

A fairly above average indie horror game that involves a pretty interesting concept with decent execution. The gameplay isn't exactly anything new nor spectacular for an indie horror game - Opening doors, solving puzzles and running away from something, but it still managed to get the job done, I never got bored with the game at any point, even at the puzzles.

The few gripes I've had, starting with the most minor: Is the lack of gameplay options that limit you to just 'running away' when being confronted, you can't exactly hide nor react accordingly to avoid an encounter; just make a mad dash from point A, to point B. The layout design of the levels aren't too bad, so most of the time you don't get lost or run into a dead end, but it still feels scripted as hell. 

Second of the gripes; are some of the puzzles, especially the ones with a time limit. Yeah, those ones can be a huge kick in the nuts but since most of the checkpoints in conjunction are very reasonable, they're not unbearable to try to complete if you get stuck. 

The worst issue for me is... the art-style, not the in-game graphics, I found it's red and grey aesthetic to be quite awesome, that it complimented the game's setting extremely well, but in a pretty jarring contrast - the artwork in the cutscenes were honest-to-god awful and very painful to look at. I'm no Artist and I doubt I can do better- but man, is it just bad; it looked like they were drawn with crayons, they were so bad that they nearly ruined the game's heavily stylised and well-established setting for me. Aside from these issues, this is still a very simple but solid indie horror that should be considered a classic, not IMSCARED levels of classic, but for me, Into the Gloom should be in the upper-echelon of indie horror games.

If you can get past the pixel-style graphics and the, in my opinion. over-reliance on jump scares in this game I think this is well worth the dirt-cheap price tag considering what you're getting. 5 different possible endings you can get, lots of notes to collect throughout the game (that unlock further lore in the main menu), a decently interesting story, a pretty spooky atmosphere, and a good soundtrack as well. 

I wouldn't say that this game is particularly "scary", unless you consider jump scares scary then this game is going to be terrifying for you, but it does retain a very dark and gloomy atmosphere and there were a few parts that I actually found to be actually scary the first time I was playing. Most reviews I've heard and read said that you'll only get about an hour or so of gameplay out of this game, but as you can see I put in 5/6 hours. That's because of the multiple endings/getting all of the notes requiring multiple playthroughs, that amount of play time for 100% is pretty good especially for an indie horror game. 

In terms of said gameplay if you were wondering about that, this is mostly a horror themed walking simulator
with puzzle-solving mixed in as well and some surprisingly well done chase-sequences. That's all there really is to say about that, this game's focus is on atmosphere and story-telling and of course constantly trying to get you with jump scares, some of which got me pretty good and some were honestly kinda pathetic.

In short, you could do a lot worse than spending several hours and a few bucks on this interesting little horror game, recommended!

Into The Gloom is an indie horror game that doesn't pull any tricks on you to get you scared. It pushes you off a cliff and gets right straight into the horror.

Graphics:
The graphics are basic 3D with pixel structures. What I love about the graphics is 95 percent of the time does not make you feel at ease. There is always something uncomfortable, whether it's from the graphics or the atmosphere. The main colors of this game are red, white, gray, and black. Most of the sky is either pitch black or a blood red. If you're into the creepypasta type of games, this will appeal to you.

Music and Sound:
I love the selection of music and sound. The eerie noises always makes me be on alert and the soundtrack makes me feel like I'm either in despair or a chaotic situation. The only problem is when picking up notes is that the sound effect is a bit too loud.

Story:
You are suddenly in a strange area and wake up in a hospital. You play as a boy named Ethan. Apparently, something happened to his brain and there is something lurking around the area and killing people. Later on, it reveals what really happened to him and where he is actually at. Obstacles and puzzles are in your way from progressing, which sometimes involve drastic measures. And...you're not alone; some beings are going to be really happy once they finally catch you.

Gameplay:
During the course of the game, there are some optional things you can do that affect your gameplay and get certain endings. You can also pick up notes in the game that you can read, plus unlock certain information on the main menu. There are some cases where you have to outrun figures in order to avoid game overs and bad endings.

Most of the puzzles are solvable...however, before the end of the game, there is a puzzle that is random. You have to line all crates in the middle in a small amount of time in order to cross. Each time you try again, they are randomized, and there is limited movement. I can understand if there are 3 random patterns to one puzzle, but random each time, and the fact you have to do it in a short amount if time is REALLY annoying.

Another thing that is annoying is at certain points of the game, you get stuck and not sure where to go next. You really have to look in every nook and cranny (except the trashcans. you'll thank me later.) in order to progress further.

So just those two things I have problem with. Otherwise, the gameplay is great.

Controls:
The controls use a lot of the keyboard and point-and-click methods. You have to use Z, X to select items, use C to combine items, right click in order to use items on objects, and left click to try to open doors and pick up notes and items. It gets tedious and hard to get used to at first, but you'll get the hang of it.

Overall:
Into The Gloom just gets to the point, which is the horror of the game. It proves that you don't need fancy graphics or many colors in order to get the feel of horror of the game. Just having the right atmosphere, music, sounds, and situation makes this into one of the masterpieces of indie horror games. If you're looking for a horror game or if you're a creepypasta enthusiast, this game will not disappoint you in the end.

Pros:
-Music that perfectly fits any situation in the game.
-Atmosphere.
-A story that goes as deep as you go.
-Optional things you can do to unlock different endings.
-Gets straight to the horror.

Cons:
-Easy to get stuck at certain points if you don't know what to do.
-That random crate puzzle at the end.
-Slightly complicated controls, but easy to catch on.
